set1.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set1.q: A 59-year-old man with three coronary stents and no valve disease needs a tooth extracted. He asks whether he needs antibiotics before the procedure. Which advice is most accurate?
opts: No prophylaxis is needed

Correct. Prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk conditions (prosthetic valves or valve-repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation); coronary stents are not among them.
Amoxicillin before every visit
Coronary stents are not a high-risk condition, so amoxicillin prophylaxis is not indicated.
Clindamycin before the visit
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of Clostridioides difficile risk, and he does not need prophylaxis at all.
Postpone until stents removed
Stents are not removed, and they do not create a need for endocarditis prophylaxis.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 75-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve needs a dental extraction. He had a mild delayed rash (no hives, swelling or anaphylaxis) with penicillin and cannot take oral medication. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Oral azithromycin
Azithromycin is an oral option, and he cannot take oral medication; cefazolin or ceftriaxone by injection fits.
Clindamycin injection
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.
Cefazolin by injection

Correct. Penicillin-allergic patients unable to take oral medication receive cefazolin or ceftriaxone intramuscularly or intravenously, provided there is no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.
Ampicillin injection
Ampicillin is a penicillin; the injectable penicillin is for patients without penicillin allergy.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 57-year-old man with native valve endocarditis is improving on intravenous antibiotics and asks whether he can switch to pills so he can go home sooner. Which reply is most accurate?
opts: Therapy stays parenteral
Correct. Antibiotics for endocarditis should be given parenterally and must be bactericidal and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture.
Pills work just as well now
Oral therapy is not the stated standard; endocarditis antibiotics are parenteral.
Two more days, then stop
Stopping early leaves bacteria alive in the vegetation; therapy is prolonged for weeks.
Only if the fever returns
The route does not depend on fever; endocarditis therapy stays parenteral and prolonged throughout the course.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 69-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter for 2 days of new confusion. She has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), a new murmur and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). Brain imaging shows multiple small scattered lesions without a large stroke. Which mechanism best explains her confusion?
opts: Low-flow ischemia from heart block
No conduction block is described; scattered lesions with fever and a murmur point to septic emboli.
A side effect of sedation
She has had no sedation; fever, a murmur, petechiae and scattered brain lesions mean septic emboli.
Septic emboli to the brain
Correct. Vegetations shower septic emboli into the systemic circulation; the brain is affected (ischemic stroke, abscess, hemorrhage, meningitis), producing neurologic deficits such as confusion.
A primary bacterial meningitis
Meningitis is one cerebral complication, but scattered small lesions with a new murmur and petechiae point to septic emboli from a vegetation.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 45-year-old woman has 2 months of fever, weight loss and fatigue. A new murmur with a tumor plop (a low-pitched early diastolic sound) is heard, and three sets of blood cultures drawn before any antibiotics are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Subacute endocarditis
Subacute endocarditis usually grows an organism in cultures drawn before antibiotics, and a tumor plop is the sign of a cardiac tumor.
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia and raised inflammatory markers, not a new murmur with a tumor plop.
Lyme disease
Lyme disease causes fever and, rarely, myocarditis; it does not produce a tumor plop.
Atrial myxoma
Correct. Atrial myxoma mimics endocarditis with fever and a new murmur, a tumor plop or mid-diastolic rumble, but it is a tumor and the cultures stay negative.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 28-year-old woman with a malar rash, painful joints and a positive antinuclear antibody test has a new murmur. She has no fever, repeated blood cultures are negative, and echocardiography shows small sterile-appearing valve vegetations. Which is the most likely cause of her valve lesion?
opts: Device endocarditis
She has no pacemaker or defibrillator. Her lupus explains a non-infective valve lesion.
Libman-Sacks endocarditis
Correct. Systemic lupus erythematosus may present with non-infective (Libman-Sacks) endocarditis, which mimics infective endocarditis in the autoimmune differential.
Subacute infective endocarditis
Without fever and with repeatedly negative cultures, a lupus patient's valve lesion is far more likely non-infective Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
Acute infective endocarditis
Acute endocarditis is hectically febrile and toxic with positive cultures, which she lacks.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 64-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis has 2 days of worsening breathlessness and orthopnea (breathlessness when lying flat). A new, loud regurgitant murmur is heard and crackles fill both lung bases. Which mechanism explains her heart failure?
opts: A toxic myocarditis from fever
Fever does not cause the heart failure described. Destroyed valve function, with a new regurgitant murmur, is the mechanism.
Fluid overload from antibiotics
Intravenous antibiotics are not the mechanism given; the new regurgitant murmur points to valvular dysfunction.
Constriction from the pericardium
Pericardial constriction is a separate disease. Endocarditis causes heart failure through valvular dysfunction.
Valvular dysfunction from infection
Correct. Congestive heart failure in infective endocarditis is due to valvular dysfunction, here from leaflet damage or chordal rupture, and it is the most common indication for surgery.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 79-year-old man has enterococcal endocarditis of the aortic valve after recurrent urinary infections. Which outcome is he at notable risk for?
opts: Septic lung emboli
Septic pulmonary emboli come from right-sided disease, typically tricuspid infection in injection drug use.
Needing valve replacement
Correct. Enterococcal endocarditis is difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance, and major complications with need for valve replacement occur in about 30-40%.
Spontaneous cure
Enterococcal endocarditis does not cure itself; it is difficult to treat because of resistance.
Lowest death rate
Enterococci are not the low-risk organism; antibiotic resistance makes them hard to treat, with valve replacement in 30-40%.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 53-year-old man has had positive blood cultures for 10 days despite an antibiotic regimen that matches his organism's sensitivities, and he still has fevers. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Switch to oral therapy
Oral step-down does not treat persistent bacteremia; therapy stays parenteral, and infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics is a surgical indication.
Stop antibiotics and observe
Stopping therapy in persistent bacteremia risks valve destruction and death; surgical evaluation is indicated instead.
Start full anticoagulation
Anticoagulation is not beneficial in native valve infection and does not clear bacteremia.
Evaluation for surgery
Correct. Infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotic therapy is an indication for surgery, as are heart failure from valve dysfunction, abscess and fungal infection.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 66-year-old man with subacute endocarditis has a fundoscopic examination that shows Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages). What process causes these spots?
opts: Vasculitis of small retinal arteries
Correct. Roth spots are white-centered hemorrhages from vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina, grouped with the immunologic phenomena in the Duke criteria.
Retinal detachment from trauma
Trauma and detachment are not the mechanism. Roth spots come from vasculitis of the small retinal arteries.
Optic nerve swelling from pressure
Raised intracranial pressure swells the optic disc; it does not make white-centered hemorrhages.
Hypertensive retinal changes
Hypertension causes its own retinopathy. Roth spots reflect vasculitis of small retinal arteries in endocarditis.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 59-year-old man with native aortic valve endocarditis and a large vegetation asks whether a blood thinner would prevent a stroke. He has no other reason for anticoagulation. Which choice should be avoided?
opts: Consulting infectious disease
Infectious disease directs antibiotics and outpatient monitoring; consulting them is appropriate.
Starting full anticoagulation
Correct. Anticoagulation is not beneficial in patients with native valve infection (it is controversial with prosthetic valves), so it should not be started for this reason.
Continuing his antibiotics
Bactericidal parenteral antibiotics are the backbone of treatment and should continue.
Monitoring renal function
Close monitoring of labs and renal function is part of endocarditis management and should continue throughout therapy.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 58-year-old woman has a fever, a new murmur and Janeway lesions (painless macules on her soles), and two blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Her transesophageal echocardiogram is read as normal. Which conclusion is correct?
opts: Endocarditis is not ruled out
Correct. A normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule out endocarditis; with a typical organism and supporting signs she is still treated as having it.
Endocarditis is now excluded
Even a highly sensitive test can miss vegetations. A normal study does not necessarily rule out endocarditis.
The cultures were contaminated
Staphylococcus aureus in two separate cultures is a typical endocarditis organism, not contamination.
She has only a skin infection
Janeway lesions are embolic (vascular) signs of endocarditis, not a skin infection, and they support the diagnosis.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 47-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F) and Janeway lesions (painless hemorrhagic macules) on the soles of both feet. Blood cultures are pending. Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Janeway lesions fall into?
opts: Immunologic phenomenon
Immunologic phenomena are glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor. Painless Janeway lesions are vascular.
Major endocardial criterion
Major endocardial evidence comes from echocardiography or new valvular regurgitation, not from skin lesions.
Microbiologic evidence
Microbiologic evidence is a culture or serologic finding; the cultures here are still pending.
Vascular phenomenon

Correct. Janeway lesions are a vascular (embolic) phenomenon, a minor criterion with major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage and conjunctival hemorrhages.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 58-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis needs a root canal. She developed hives (urticaria) after amoxicillin years ago and can take pills. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Oral amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is a penicillin and caused her hives, so it is avoided; a macrolide such as azithromycin is used instead.
Oral clindamycin
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.
Oral azithromycin
Correct. A penicillin-allergic patient who can take oral medication gets azithromycin or clarithromycin, or doxycycline; cephalexin is avoided after urticaria to penicillin.
Oral cephalexin
Cephalosporins should not be used after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillin, and she had hives.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 62-year-old man with fever, a new murmur and positive blood cultures is stable. A transthoracic study is limited by his body habitus. Which imaging test best detects vegetations and defines the extent of disease?
opts: Transesophageal echocardiogram
Correct. Transesophageal echocardiography is highly sensitive and specific, detects vegetations on the valve leaflets and defines the extent of disease.
Repeat transthoracic study
Repeating a limited transthoracic study adds little; the transesophageal study is the highly sensitive and specific one.
Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph cannot show valve vegetations; the transesophageal echocardiogram detects them and defines extent.
Coronary angiography
Angiography images the coronary arteries, not valve vegetations; transesophageal echocardiography shows them.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 60-year-old woman with a prosthetic valve and a past episode of anaphylaxis to penicillin needs a dental cleaning and can take pills. Which prophylactic agent should be avoided?
opts: Clarithromycin
Clarithromycin is an appropriate oral option for a penicillin-allergic patient, even after anaphylaxis to penicillin.
Doxycycline
Doxycycline is an appropriate oral option for a penicillin-allergic patient, even after anaphylaxis to penicillin.
Cephalexin
Correct. Cephalexin, cefazolin and ceftriaxone should not be used in patients with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria to penicillin or ampicillin.
Azithromycin
Azithromycin is an appropriate oral option for a penicillin-allergic patient, even after anaphylaxis to penicillin.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: An 85-year-old man with degenerative aortic valve disease presents with fever and a new murmur. His family is surprised that a heart infection could occur at his age. Which statement is accurate?
opts: It occurs only in drug users
Injection drug use is one risk factor, but more than half of cases occur in people over 60.
It occurs only in children
Pediatric endocarditis has low incidence; most cases are in older adults, with over-60s more than half.
Age lowers the risk
Age raises the risk rather than lowering it: patients over 60 make up more than half of all cases.
Over-60s are over half of cases
Correct. Risk is increased among the elderly: patients over 60 account for more than 50% of cases, and degenerative valve disease is now a leading predisposing condition.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 61-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis develops worsening breathlessness, crackles and a new loud regurgitant murmur on day 3 of appropriate antibiotics. Echocardiography shows a ruptured chord with severe regurgitation. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Outpatient cardiology
This is a hospital problem needing urgent surgical evaluation, not an outpatient visit.
Cardiothoracic surgery
Correct. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery, and cardiothoracic surgery evaluates the need for surgery.
Addiction medicine
Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs; it does not address valve failure.
Palliative care alone
Palliative care may join a multidisciplinary plan, but heart failure from valve dysfunction calls for surgical evaluation.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 44-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F) and Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages) on fundoscopy, meeting three minor Duke criteria. He has received no antibiotics. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Order a chest radiograph and discharge
A chest radiograph cannot show vegetations. He needs blood cultures and echocardiography, not discharge.
Draw blood cultures from separate sites
Correct. Blood cultures (three sets from separate sites) come before any antibiotic; a positive culture with a typical organism would add a major criterion and make the case definite.
Start oral amoxicillin and recheck later
Oral amoxicillin is dental prophylaxis, not treatment, and antibiotics before cultures can leave the cultures negative.
Reassure him that it is not endocarditis
Three minor criteria make endocarditis possible, and possible cases are treated as endocarditis; reassurance is inappropriate.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman in urgent care has a fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages (dark lines under the nail plates). Before transfer, a colleague proposes giving a dose of ceftriaxone right away. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Drawing three sets of cultures
Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites are exactly what she needs before any antibiotic.
Arranging hospital admission
Endocarditis is managed in hospital with parenteral antibiotics and close monitoring, so admission is appropriate.
Requesting an echocardiogram
Echocardiography is part of the workup, looking for vegetations; it should not be avoided.
Giving antibiotics before cultures
Correct. Empiric therapy is started only after blood cultures have been drawn; antibiotics given first may sterilize the cultures and lose the organism.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 65-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve has a fever of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F). Three blood cultures grow viridans streptococci, and a transesophageal echocardiogram shows new partial dehiscence of the prosthesis. How many major Duke criteria does he meet?
opts: No major criteria
Typical organisms in separate cultures and new prosthetic dehiscence are both major criteria.
Three major criteria
There are only two major criteria (blood culture and endocardial involvement); he meets both.
Two major criteria
Correct. A typical organism in separate cultures is one major criterion, and new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve on echocardiogram is the second; two major criteria make the case definite.
One major criterion
Both the cultures and the echocardiographic dehiscence are major criteria, so he meets two.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: A 4-month-old with tachycardia, poor feeding, respiratory distress and hypotension is being worked up for sepsis. A new murmur is heard. Why must endocarditis be considered even though the presentation looks like sepsis?
opts: Infant endocarditis mimics sepsis

Correct. In neonates and infants endocarditis presents nonspecifically and is often indistinguishable from sepsis or heart failure: feeding difficulty, respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension and a new or changing murmur.
Infants show classic Osler nodes
Classic peripheral stigmata are considerably less common in children, so their absence does not exclude endocarditis.
Infants always have joint pain
Arthralgias belong to the indolent course of older children, not to infants, who present like sepsis.
Sepsis never causes tachycardia
Sepsis does cause tachycardia; the point is that infant endocarditis looks like sepsis.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with native mitral valve endocarditis after dental work has blood cultures growing penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci. Which antibiotic is a directed choice?
opts: Nafcillin or oxacillin
Nafcillin and oxacillin are antistaphylococcal penicillins for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.
Rifampin plus gentamicin
Rifampin and gentamicin are add-ons for staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection, not the streptococcal backbone.
Daptomycin alone
Daptomycin is an option for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, not the directed streptococcal choice.
Penicillin G or ceftriaxone
Correct. Viridans streptococci are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin, or vancomycin if penicillin cannot be used.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 71-year-old man had his aortic valve replaced 6 weeks ago. He now has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F) and a new regurgitant murmur, and transesophageal imaging shows a vegetation on the prosthesis. Which organisms are most likely?
opts: Enterococci from urine
Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract; early prosthetic valve infection is staphylococcal.
Airway gram-negatives
The upper-airway HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms are not the early prosthetic valve organisms; staphylococci are.
Staphylococci from the skin

Correct. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis is caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus, skin organisms introduced around the time of surgery.
Viridans streptococci
Viridans streptococci cause late prosthetic valve endocarditis; at 6 weeks the organisms are staphylococci.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 70-year-old man has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and malaise that began a week after a dental extraction. A new murmur of mitral regurgitation is heard. Three sets of blood cultures are drawn. Which organism are they most likely to grow?
opts: Candida species
Candida causes fungal endocarditis in the immunocompromised and in patients with central lines, not subacute disease after a tooth extraction.
Viridans streptococci
Correct. The oral cavity is the source of viridans streptococci, the classic cause of subacute endocarditis after dental procedures and the organism dental prophylaxis targets.
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is a skin organism that causes acute, toxic disease; a smoldering course after dental work points to viridans streptococci.
Enterococci
Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract, not the mouth; an oral source after dental work brings viridans streptococci.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 67-year-old woman has had 2 months of low-grade fevers to 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), fatigue and a 4-kilogram weight loss. She had a tooth extracted 10 weeks ago. A new apical systolic murmur is heard, and splinter hemorrhages (thin dark lines under the nail plates) are seen on two fingers. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute infective endocarditis
Acute disease is abrupt and toxic over 3-10 days with high fevers. Two months of low-grade fever and weight loss is subacute.
Subacute infective endocarditis

Correct. An indolent course with lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks to months, a new murmur, splinter hemorrhages and a dental source fits subacute endocarditis, classically from viridans streptococci.
Pulmonary tuberculosis
Tuberculosis causes fever, night sweats and weight loss, but not a new murmur with splinter hemorrhages after dental work.
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia with high inflammatory markers; it does not produce a new murmur or splinter hemorrhages.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 29-year-old woman who injects drugs has 5 days of high fever and rigors. Transthoracic imaging shows a large vegetation on the tricuspid valve, and three sets of blood cultures are drawn from separate sites. Which organism are the cultures most likely to grow?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus

Correct. In people who inject drugs, Staphylococcus aureus causes more than 60% of all endocarditis and 80-90% of cases where the tricuspid valve is infected, so methicillin resistance must be assumed until proven otherwise.
Viridans streptococci
Viridans streptococci follow oral sources such as dental work. Injection through the skin introduces Staphylococcus aureus.
Enterococcus faecalis
Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract. Tricuspid endocarditis in a person who injects drugs is Staphylococcus aureus in 80-90%.
Candida albicans
Candida is a fungal cause linked to immunocompromise and central lines; the dominant organism in injection drug use is Staphylococcus aureus.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: A 4-year-old with cyanotic congenital heart disease and a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt has 2 weeks of fever. The murmur sounds unchanged. Which finding would most suggest that the shunt is infected?
opts: Osler nodes on fingers
Classic peripheral stigmata are considerably less common in children than in adults.
Rising blood pressure
Rising blood pressure is not the listed sign of shunt infection; falling oxygen saturation is.
Falling oxygen saturation
Correct. In children with cyanotic congenital heart disease and systemic-pulmonary shunts the murmur may not change; falling oxygen saturation can signal graft infection.
An unchanged murmur
An unchanged murmur is expected in these children and does not exclude infection.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 46-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) and Janeway lesions (painless macules) on his palms. A transesophageal echocardiogram shows an oscillating mass on the tricuspid valve. Blood cultures are still pending. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Definite endocarditis

Correct. One major criterion (the oscillating mass on echocardiogram) plus three minor criteria (injection drug use as predisposition, fever, and Janeway lesions as a vascular phenomenon) make endocarditis definite.
Possible endocarditis
One major plus one minor would be possible, but he has one major plus three minor criteria, which is definite.
Rejected endocarditis
No alternative diagnosis has been made and no antibiotics have been given; nothing rejects the diagnosis.
Not classifiable yet
Pending cultures do not prevent classification; one major and three minor criteria already make it definite.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: A 12-year-old had a ventricular septal defect closed with a prosthetic patch 4 months ago and is now scheduled for a dental extraction. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Give antibiotics afterward
Prophylaxis is given before the procedure so the drug is circulating during the bacteremia.
Give prophylaxis beforehand
Correct. The first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device is a high-risk period, and extraction manipulates the gums, so prophylaxis is given.
No prophylaxis is needed
Within 6 months of repair with prosthetic material, the child is high risk and prophylaxis is indicated.
Delay the extraction a year
Delay is not the recommendation; a prophylactic dose before the extraction is, during the 6-month high-risk window.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 74-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections was treated for pyelonephritis a month ago. She now has low-grade fevers, fatigue and a new murmur, and blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Viridans streptococci
Viridans streptococci come from the oral cavity; a genitourinary source points to enterococci.
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Coagulase-negative staphylococci such as Staphylococcus epidermidis are skin organisms tied to early prosthetic valve and device infection, not urinary sources.
Streptococcus gallolyticus
Streptococcus gallolyticus comes from the gastrointestinal tract. The urinary source organism is enterococci.
Enterococci
Correct. The genitourinary tract is the source of enterococci, which cause subacute and native valve endocarditis; urinary tract infection gives them a route into the blood.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 59-year-old man with suspected endocarditis is too unstable to undergo a transesophageal study today. A transthoracic echocardiogram is available now. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Obtain the transthoracic study now
Correct. Transesophageal echocardiography is preferred for its sensitivity, but a transthoracic study can still show a large vegetation and should not be withheld while waiting.
Skip imaging entirely
Echocardiography is part of the major criteria; skipping imaging removes evidence of endocardial involvement.
Wait two weeks to image
Waiting risks progressive valve destruction; image with what is available and treat after cultures.
Order a chest radiograph instead
A chest radiograph cannot show vegetations; echocardiography can, and a transthoracic study is acceptable when the patient is unstable.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman with viridans streptococcal endocarditis had positive blood cultures on days 1 and 2 and her first negative culture on day 4. She asks how long her antibiotics will last. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Until her fever settles
Defervescence does not end therapy; the course is 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture.
4-6 weeks from the day 4 culture
Correct. Therapy is typically 4-6 weeks counted from the first negative culture, here day 4, because all bacteria in the vegetation must be killed.
4-6 weeks from admission day
The clock does not start at admission; it starts at the first negative blood culture, which here was day 4.
10 days from the first dose
Ten days is far too short to sterilize a vegetation; therapy runs 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 49-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever and night sweats. Two separate blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus, and a transesophageal echocardiogram shows an oscillating mass on the aortic valve. He has no skin, eye or kidney findings. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Possible endocarditis
Possible is one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. He has two major criteria, which is definite.
Rejected endocarditis
Nothing rejects the diagnosis: there is no alternative diagnosis and no resolution within 4 days of antibiotics.
Unclassifiable for now
No further test is needed to classify him; two major criteria already make the diagnosis definite.
Definite endocarditis

Correct. Two major criteria are met: a typical organism (Streptococcus gallolyticus) in two separate cultures and an oscillating mass on echocardiogram. Two major criteria alone establish definite endocarditis.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 56-year-old man on chemotherapy has Candida endocarditis confirmed on blood cultures and echocardiography. Which referral is most appropriate in addition to infectious disease?
opts: Dermatology
Dermatology has no role in fungal valve infection; cardiothoracic surgery evaluates the need for an operation.
Cardiothoracic surgery
Correct. Fungal infection is difficult to cure with medications alone and is an indication for surgery, so cardiothoracic surgery evaluates him.
Addiction medicine
Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs; he has fungal infection needing surgical evaluation instead.
Physical therapy
Rehabilitation may come later, but fungal endocarditis needs surgical evaluation now.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman with aortic valve endocarditis has a transesophageal echocardiogram that shows an abscess around the valve ring. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Oral step-down now
Oral therapy is not appropriate; an abscess calls for surgical evaluation with continued parenteral antibiotics.
Repeat echo in 6 months
Waiting months allows the abscess to destroy tissue around the valve; abscess is an indication for surgery now.
Surgical evaluation
Correct. Abscess is an indication for surgery; antibiotics penetrate abscesses poorly, so cardiothoracic surgery evaluates her.
Shorten antibiotics
An abscess makes the infection complicated; shortening therapy is never appropriate here.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 71-year-old woman with suspected endocarditis has a urinalysis sent as part of her workup. Which urinalysis result is most consistent with endocarditis?
opts: Glucose and ketones only
Glucose and ketones point to diabetes, not endocarditis, whose urinalysis shows hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria.
Bilirubin and urobilinogen
Urine bilirubin and urobilinogen point to liver or hemolytic disease, not endocarditis.
Nitrites alone, no cells
Nitrites without cells is not the pattern; hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria are.
Blood, protein and white cells
Correct. Urinalysis in endocarditis can show hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria, reflecting renal involvement such as glomerulonephritis or emboli.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 59-year-old man is on day 6 of antibiotics for aortic valve endocarditis. He still has fevers, and today's electrocardiogram shows a new conduction block not present on admission. Which complication best explains the new conduction abnormality?
opts: Chordae tendineae rupture
Chordal rupture causes a new regurgitant murmur and heart failure, not a conduction block.
Septal perivalvular abscess
Correct. When infection extends beyond the leaflets into the myocardium as a perivalvular abscess and reaches the upper ventricular septum, it interrupts the conduction system.
Septic emboli to the lungs
Pulmonary septic emboli come from right-sided vegetations and cause cough and pleuritic pain, not conduction block.
Spread into the epicardium
Extension into the epicardium causes pericarditis. Conduction block follows extension into the upper ventricular septum.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 50-year-old woman with fever and a soft murmur was started on antibiotics for suspected endocarditis. After 3 days her fever is gone, her symptoms have resolved and do not recur, and an alternative source is found. How is the suspected endocarditis classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Rejected
Correct. Endocarditis is rejected when an alternative diagnosis is established, or when symptoms resolve and do not recur with 4 days or less of antibiotic therapy.
Possible
Possible requires one major plus one minor or three minor criteria without a rejecting finding; resolution within 4 days rejects it.
Definite
Definite requires two major, one major and three minor, or five minor criteria; nothing here meets that.
Recurrent
Recurrence is not a Duke category. Rapid resolution with an alternative diagnosis rejects endocarditis.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 41-year-old man who injects drugs is being treated for tricuspid valve endocarditis. On day 2 he develops a new cough and sharp chest pain on inspiration, and imaging shows new nodular infiltrates in both lungs. Which complication best explains these findings?
opts: Left heart failure
Heart failure from valve dysfunction floods the lungs diffusely; it does not cause scattered nodules with pleuritic pain. Septic emboli do.
Aspiration of vomit
Aspiration causes a dependent pneumonia, not scattered bilateral nodules in a patient with a tricuspid vegetation.
Septic pulmonary emboli
Correct. Tricuspid vegetations throw septic emboli into the pulmonary circulation, causing cough and pleuritic chest pain, with nodular infiltrates on imaging; empyema can follow.
Drug-induced lung injury
Antibiotic lung toxicity is not the mechanism described. Right-sided vegetations shed septic emboli to the lungs.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 77-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. His son asks how serious this organism is. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: It is the most lethal organism
Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism in endocarditis, with mortality highest in prosthetic valve endocarditis (about 50%).
It carries a good prognosis
A relatively good prognosis belongs to viridans streptococci treated before complications, not Staphylococcus aureus.
It rarely needs any surgery
Prosthetic valve staphylococcal infection is severe; surgery is evaluated by cardiothoracic surgery when indicated.
It resolves within a week
Therapy alone runs weeks (typically 4-6 from the first negative culture), and the infection is the most lethal kind.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin has 4 days of fever to 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), rigors, a cough and sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breaths. A holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border, and a chest radiograph shows several small nodular infiltrates in both lungs. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute viral pericarditis
Pericarditis brings positional pain and a friction rub, not a holosystolic murmur, rigors and nodular lung infiltrates.
Tricuspid valve endocarditis

Correct. Injected bacteria enter the venous circulation and reach the right heart first, so the tricuspid valve is infected; its vegetation throws septic emboli to the lungs, causing cough, pleuritic pain and nodular infiltrates.
Community-acquired pneumonia
Pneumonia would not explain a new right-sided murmur in a person who injects drugs, nor multiple scattered nodules; these point to septic emboli from a tricuspid vegetation.
Mitral valve endocarditis
Mitral vegetations embolize to the systemic circulation (brain, kidneys, skin), not the lungs. Pulmonary nodules point to the right-sided tricuspid valve.

set2.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set2.q: A 52-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve is booked for a diagnostic bronchoscopy. No biopsy or mucosal incision is planned. Which advice about endocarditis prophylaxis is most accurate?
opts: None is needed for this procedure
Correct. Bronchoscopy does not require prophylaxis unless it involves incision of the respiratory mucosa, such as a biopsy.
Required before every bronchoscopy
Plain bronchoscopy is on the list that does not need prophylaxis; only mucosal incision or biopsy changes that.
A week of oral amoxicillin
Prophylaxis is never a week-long course, and none is needed for this bronchoscopy.
Intravenous vancomycin first
Vancomycin is not the standard prophylaxis and none is needed for this bronchoscopy.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 60-year-old woman has viridans streptococcal endocarditis diagnosed early, before any heart failure or abscess, and she starts appropriate antibiotics the same day. Which statement about her outlook is most accurate?
opts: Valve replacement in most
A 30-40% valve replacement rate is described for enterococcal endocarditis, not early-treated viridans streptococci.
Death within weeks is likely
Death within weeks describes untreated acute endocarditis, not early-treated viridans streptococcal disease.
Relatively good prognosis
Correct. Viridans streptococcal endocarditis has a relatively good prognosis if antibiotic treatment starts before complications occur.
Highest mortality of any
Highest mortality belongs to Staphylococcus aureus, especially on prosthetic valves.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman being evaluated for endocarditis had a soft systolic murmur documented for 10 years. Today the murmur sounds a little louder. How does this change count under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: It is an immunologic phenomenon
Immunologic phenomena are glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor, not murmur changes.
It confirms definite endocarditis
A louder old murmur adds nothing toward the major criterion and cannot confirm the diagnosis.
It does not meet the major criterion
Correct. New valvular regurgitation counts as endocardial involvement, but an increase or change in a preexisting murmur is not sufficient.
It meets the major criterion
Only new valvular regurgitation meets the criterion; a louder preexisting murmur is specifically not sufficient.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 72-year-old woman has 6 weeks of aching and stiffness in her shoulders and hips, fatigue and a low-grade fever. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are high, but no murmur is heard and three sets of blood cultures are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Subacute endocarditis
Subacute endocarditis brings a new murmur and positive cultures in most patients; neither is present here.
Atrial myxoma
Atrial myxoma would give fever with a new murmur, such as a tumor plop; she has no murmur.
Antiphospholipid syndrome
Antiphospholipid syndrome mimics endocarditis through thromboemboli and valve disease, not girdle myalgia.
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Correct. Polymyalgia rheumatica sits in the differential of endocarditis because it causes myalgia with elevated inflammatory markers, but there is no murmur and cultures are negative.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set2.q: A 9-year-old with unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is scheduled for a tonsillectomy. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Give antibiotics only afterward
Prophylaxis is given before the procedure so the drug is circulating when bacteremia occurs.
Cancel all future surgery
Surgery need not be canceled; a single prophylactic dose before the tonsillectomy is the recommended approach.
Give prophylaxis before surgery

Correct. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is a high-risk pediatric condition, and tonsillectomy is an invasive respiratory procedure with mucosal incision, so prophylaxis is given beforehand.
No prophylaxis is needed
Both the condition and the procedure qualify: high-risk heart disease plus incision of respiratory mucosa.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set2.q: A 2-month-old infant with a central line has poor feeding, fast breathing, tachycardia and a changing murmur. Blood cultures are positive and echocardiography shows a vegetation. Which complications are particularly common in infants because of septic emboli?
opts: Glomerulonephritis only
Glomerulonephritis is an immunologic sign, not the listed infant complication of septic emboli.
Osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia
Correct. Septic emboli are common in neonates and infants, producing osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia, and neurologic signs such as seizures, hemiparesis and apnea.
Janeway lesions and Roth spots
Classic peripheral stigmata are considerably less common in children; infants' septic emboli cause osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia.
Heart failure from valve stenosis
Pediatric endocarditis causes less heart failure than adult disease; septic emboli are the infant problem.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: An 83-year-old woman is ready for discharge on day 9 of a planned 6-week course of intravenous antibiotics for endocarditis. She is deconditioned and cannot yet walk safely on her own. Which part of the multidisciplinary plan addresses this?
opts: Stopping the antibiotics
Antibiotics continue for the full course; rehabilitation addresses her mobility.
Rehabilitation placement
Correct. The multidisciplinary team plans disposition, including rehabilitation, while infectious disease continues antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring.
Addiction medicine
Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs, not deconditioning.
Immediate valve surgery
Deconditioning is not a surgical indication; surgery is for heart failure, abscess, persistent infection or fungi.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 52-year-old woman on long-term immunosuppression has endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow Candida. Which complication is most likely?
opts: Embolic large artery occlusion
Correct. In fungal endocarditis the most likely complication is embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries from embolization.
Rapid cure with medication
Fungal endocarditis is difficult to cure with medications alone and is an indication for surgery.
Isolated rheumatic carditis
Rheumatic carditis is an immune reaction to streptococci, not a complication of Candida endocarditis.
Pericardial knock
A pericardial knock belongs to constrictive pericarditis; fungal endocarditis embolizes to large arteries.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 68-year-old man with a native mitral valve has 5 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue and a new murmur. Three sets of blood cultures have just been drawn, and the organism is not yet known. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone

Correct. Empiric therapy covers staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci; vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is the regimen for a subacute presentation, native valve endocarditis, or a prosthetic valve in place more than a year.
Oral amoxicillin, single dose
A single oral dose of amoxicillin is dental prophylaxis, not treatment of established endocarditis, which needs prolonged parenteral therapy.
Nafcillin plus rifampin
Nafcillin with rifampin belongs to directed therapy for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve, not empiric native valve therapy.
Oral doxycycline for 2 weeks
Oral, short therapy cannot sterilize a vegetation; endocarditis needs bactericidal, parenteral, prolonged therapy.

set2.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set2.q: A 63-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve is having a tooth extracted tomorrow. He has no drug allergies and takes pills without difficulty. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: No prophylaxis is needed
A prosthetic valve is a high-risk condition, and extraction manipulates gums and roots, so prophylaxis is indicated.
Oral amoxicillin, 30-60 minutes before
Correct. A high-risk patient (prosthetic valve) having an extraction gets a single dose of oral amoxicillin 30-60 minutes before the procedure, targeting viridans streptococci.
Oral amoxicillin for 7 days after
Prophylaxis is a single dose given before the procedure, not a week of antibiotics afterward.
Clindamycin before the visit
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: An 81-year-old man had his pacemaker generator changed 3 weeks ago. He now has a fever of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), and imaging shows a vegetation on a pacemaker lead. Which organisms cause the largest share of this type of endocarditis?
opts: Coagulase-negative staphylococci

Correct. Device endocarditis is caused mostly by coagulase-negative staphylococci (about 41%) and Staphylococcus aureus (about 36%), and it can appear within weeks of implantation or a generator change.
Viridans streptococci
Streptococci cause only about 2% of device endocarditis; skin staphylococci dominate.
Gram-negative coccobacilli
The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms are not recorded in device infection; coagulase-negative staphylococci lead.
Enterococci
Enterococci cause about 4% of device endocarditis, far behind coagulase-negative staphylococci.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 38-year-old man who injects drugs has finished a course of intravenous antibiotics for tricuspid valve endocarditis and is preparing for discharge. He says he wants help to stay safe. Which consultation should be arranged?
opts: Dermatology
Dermatology has no listed role; harm reduction for injection drug use comes from addiction medicine.
Ophthalmology
Ophthalmology is not the consult for his drug use. Addiction medicine provides harm reduction.
Nephrology
Renal function is monitored during antibiotics, but harm reduction for injection drug use is addiction medicine's role.
Addiction medicine
Correct. Addiction medicine is consulted for harm reduction in people who inject drugs, part of the multidisciplinary care with infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman had a mechanical mitral valve placed 4 years ago. She has 5 weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue, and blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely in her prosthetic valve infection?
opts: Escherichia coli
Gram-negative bacilli are uncommon causes of endocarditis. Late prosthetic valve infection is viridans streptococcal.
Viridans streptococci
Correct. Late prosthetic valve endocarditis is caused by viridans streptococci, while early infection (around surgery) is caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus.
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Staphylococcus epidermidis is the classic early prosthetic valve organism; 4 years out, viridans streptococci are expected.
Candida albicans
Candida causes fungal endocarditis, mostly with immunocompromise or central lines; the late prosthetic valve organism is viridans streptococci.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 62-year-old man with fever has four sets of blood cultures drawn. One set grows coagulase-negative staphylococci, and the other three are negative. How should this single positive culture be counted under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: As the major blood culture criterion
The major criterion needs a typical organism in two separate cultures or persistent bacteremia, not one culture of a common contaminant.
As a vascular phenomenon
Vascular phenomena are embolic findings such as Janeway lesions, not culture results.
As definite proof of endocarditis
One culture of a common contaminant proves nothing; it is excluded from the criteria.
Not counted, a likely contaminant
Correct. Single positive cultures for coagulase-negative staphylococci (and diphtheroids) are excluded from the microbiologic criterion because they are common culture contaminants.

set2.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis brings an old wallet card that lists clindamycin for her dental prophylaxis. She has a penicillin allergy. Which counseling point is most accurate?
opts: Keep using clindamycin
The recommendation changed: clindamycin was dropped because of Clostridioides difficile risk.
Switch to amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is a penicillin and is avoided in her penicillin allergy; azithromycin or clarithromycin can be used.
She no longer needs any
Previous endocarditis remains a high-risk condition, so prophylaxis is still needed.
Clindamycin is dropped
Correct. Clindamycin is no longer recommended for prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection; she should be given an alternative such as azithromycin.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 55-year-old man has 3 days of fever to 40.0 °C (104.0 °F), rigors and a new murmur, and he looks toxic. Which organism is a classic cause of this tempo of infective endocarditis?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus
Correct. An abrupt, toxic, high-fever course is acute endocarditis, caused by virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and beta-hemolytic streptococci.
Viridans streptococci
Viridans streptococci cause subacute disease with low fevers over weeks, not a toxic course over 3 days.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci
Coagulase-negative staphylococci are listed with the subacute organisms and with early prosthetic valve infection; a classic acute organism is Staphylococcus aureus.
Gram-negative coccobacilli
The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group causes subacute endocarditis, not the acute toxic form.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has native valve endocarditis from penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci. The team discusses a 2-week regimen that adds gentamicin. Which choice should be avoided?
opts: Ceftriaxone for the full course
Ceftriaxone is a standard directed agent for viridans streptococci and does not depend on gentamicin.
Monitoring renal function
Close monitoring of labs and renal function is part of endocarditis management, especially with kidney disease.
The 2-week gentamicin regimen

Correct. The 2-week regimen with gentamicin is reserved for uncomplicated endocarditis with a rapid response and no chronic kidney disease; gentamicin is nephrotoxic, so he needs a standard course without it.
Penicillin G for the full course
Penicillin G is a standard directed agent for viridans streptococci and is appropriate for him.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with acute endocarditis asks why the team is so worried when she felt well a week ago. Which statement about untreated acute endocarditis is accurate?
opts: It smolders harmlessly for years
Smoldering for months is the subacute form; acute disease is rapidly destructive.
It only threatens the lungs
Acute disease damages the valves and seeds many extracardiac sites, not only the lungs.
It can be fatal within weeks
Correct. Acute endocarditis rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites; if untreated, it progresses to death within weeks.
It resolves without treatment
Acute endocarditis does not resolve on its own; untreated, it progresses to death within weeks.
